title.en: Adam and Eve Meet at Arafat
title.zh: 阿丹與哈娃於阿拉法特重逢

region.en: Mount Arafat, near Mecca (traditional site of the reunion; literal pin)
region.zh: 麥加附近阿拉法特山（傳統重逢地；實際定位）

texts.period: Qisas al-Anbiya tradition (Arabic, c. 8th-11th centuries CE); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Muhammad al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Tales of the Prophets), Arabic c. 1100; cf. Thackston 1978 translation (cited for reference; passages paraphrased from Arabic)

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: After the expulsion from Eden, Adam descends, the legend says, in India or Serendib and Eve on the Arabian shore; for two hundred years they wander the earth seeking one another. Where their paths finally cross, a mountain called Arafat — 'he knew' — rises; God accepts the prayer of the pair, ordains the pilgrimage round the House, and teaches Adam the rites of the hajj, which are performed on this ground to this day.
summary.zh: 相傳出園之後，阿丹降於印度或楞伽島，哈娃降於阿拉伯海岸；二人尋覓相望二百年。其行跡交會之山名為阿拉法特——『他知道了』——主應允二人之祈，命環繞天房之朝，並教阿丹朝覲之儀——即今日此地所行者。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend of a living tradition; such tales are regarded within Islam as edifying but not authoritative; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: When the two were sent down from the Garden, they were separated: Adam, it is said, came down on a mountain of Ceylon, and Eve on the shore of Arabia. Each wandered over the earth asking after the other, weeping and repenting, until at last they met in a valley of the mountains of Arabia; and the place was called Arafat, 'the place of knowing,' because there each one knew the other again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: God forgave them there and commanded Adam to build the House. He taught him the rites of the pilgrimage — the tawaf around the Kaaba, the run between the two hills, the stand at Arafat — and appointed the seasons of the sacred months. And the pilgrims stand at Arafat every year on the ninth of Dhu'l-Hijja, on the ground where the first human pair were rejoined.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

region.zh: 阿丹子孫之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Qisas al-Anbiya tradition (Arabic, c. 8th-11th centuries CE); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Muhammad al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic c. 1100); passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: After Adam's death the succession passes to Seth, the pure son, whom God had set in his father's place: to him are given fifty books of wisdom, and he teaches his people the worship of God, the reckoning of the sun and the moon, and the craft of prophecy — until his line is corrupted in the days before the Flood.
summary.zh: 阿丹歿後，其統緒傳於純潔之子塞特——主立之於其父之位：賜其五十卷智慧之書；他教人民敬拜主、推算日月、承先知之藝——直至洪水前其世系墮落。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend of a living tradition; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: When Adam died, God set Seth in his place as a prophet over his children, and gave him fifty books, in which were written the wisdom of the ages, the reckoning of the sun and the moon and the stars, and the signs of the times. Seth taught his people to worship God and to shun the works of Cain's line, which had begun to build cities and to make instruments of iron and song.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seth prophesied of the Flood and of the coming of the messengers, and taught his sons the names of the prophets to come, from Noah to the Seal. And when he died he was gathered to his father's grave in the mountain; and his people kept the faith for a season, until the sons of men took the daughters of the descendants of Cain, and the worship of God grew cold before the Flood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: The Donkey, the Name of God, and the Stowaway of the Ark
title.zh: 驢、主之名與方舟偷渡者

region.en: Mount Judi, landing of the Ark (traditional site; literal pin)
region.zh: 朱迪山——方舟停靠地（傳統地點；實際定位）

texts.period: Qisas al-Anbiya tradition (Arabic, c. 8th-11th centuries CE); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Muhammad al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic c. 1100); passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: The beasts are gathered two by two; but one creature will not board — a donkey in whom the Evil One is hidden. Noah cries 'In the name of God, get in!', and the demon is driven out — and in shame of his flight, Satan clutches the donkey's tail, which stands up on end from that day. Of the two ravens and the dove; of the dog that guarded the ark; and of the hog that Noah formed of the elephant's — these are the legendary deck-mates of the Flood.
summary.zh: 獸類成雙登舟；惟一獸不願登——驢，魔匿於其中。努哈呼『奉主之名，進來！』——魔被驅出；魔羞而攫驢之尾，故驢尾自是翹起。二鴉與鴿；守舟之犬；以及由象所造之豬——此皆洪水的傳奇艙友。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend of a living tradition; the Satan-in-the-donkey tale is classic popular qisas; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: When the creatures were gathered into the ark, one would not go in: a donkey at whom Satan had hidden. Noah dragged it, and it brayed and hung back; then Noah said, 'In the name of God, get in!' and the demon fled from the donkey. But as he fled, Satan clutched the donkey's tail with his hand, and it stood on end from that day — and this is why men say the braying of the ass is the voice of the Evil One.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: Noah sent out two ravens to seek the dry land, and a dove; and the dove returned with a green leaf in its beak. And among the creatures of the ark was a dog that is said to have guarded the door, and the pair of swine; and the legend tells that the hog was formed of the elephant and called swine, that its flesh might be a medicine against the serpent's venom. When the water sank the ark came to rest on Mount Judi, and Noah and his household came forth upon the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: Azazil: Iblis Among the Angels of the First Heaven
title.zh: 阿扎齊勒：初天的天使易卜劣廝

region.en: Lower heaven of the angels (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 天使的低層天（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Qisas al-Anbiya tradition (Arabic, c. 8th-11th centuries CE); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Muhammad al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic c. 1100); passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: Before Adam there were jinn, made of smokeless fire, who wasted the earth with blood; God sent an army of angels against them, and among the captives was a youth named Azazil, who worshipped God with such devotion that he was raised into the lower heaven and taught the angels. When Adam was created, God said 'Bow down'; and Azazil — the proudest of the worshippers — could not bow to a thing of clay: 'I am better than he; Thou hast created me of fire and him of clay.' And pride was the first sin.
summary.zh: 阿丹之前有精靈，由無煙之火所造，以血染地；主遣天使軍征之，俘中有名阿扎齊勒之青年，拜主至誠，被擢於低層天，教授天使。阿丹受造，主命俯首；阿扎齊勒——最傲的敬拜者——不能向黏土之身俯首：『我比他尊貴；你以火造我，以土造他。』傲慢乃第一罪。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend of a living tradition; the name Azazil and the jinn backstory come from tafsir/qisas lore; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: Before the children of Adam the jinn walked the earth, made of the smokeless fire, and they shed blood and corrupted it. God sent down an army of angels, and they fought them and took captives; and among the captives was a youth of wonderful beauty, called Azazil. He was raised to the lower heaven and taught the angels, and worshipped God with the angels; and there was none among them more devout than he.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: When God created Adam from clay and breathed into him of His spirit, He said to the angels, 'Bow down'; and they bowed, all of them, but Azazil refused and was too proud, and said, 'I am better than he: Thou hast created me of fire, and him of clay.' Then God said, 'Get thee down from it, for thou art not to glorify Me here'; and the worshipper of many years became the Accursed, and the first sin in heaven was pride.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: Harut and Marut: The Two Angels of Babylon
title.zh: 哈魯特與馬魯特：巴比倫的兩位天使

region.en: Babylon, between heaven and earth (literal pin)
region.zh: 巴比倫，天地之間（實際定位）

texts.period: Qur'an 2:102 with Qisas/tafsir expansions (Arabic); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Qur'an 2:102 with Qisas al-Anbiya / tafsir legends (al-Kisa'i; al-Tha'alabi); passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: The angels marvel that men sin so; God names two of them to be sent down and given the desires of men. Harut and Marut descend to Babylon in the form of men, and are undone by a woman — one named Zuhra, who demands wine, idolatry and murder of them before she will hear the greatest name of God. They fall; the Name escapes them; and they hang head-down between heaven and earth until the Day of Resurrection, where they teach magic to whoever comes to them in Babylon — warning all who learn: 'We are a trial; do not disbelieve.'
summary.zh: 天使訝異人類之罪；主遣二天使下降，賦以人之欲。哈魯特與馬魯特化身為人降至巴比倫，毀於一女子——名祖赫拉者，她要先得酒、偶像與殺人，方肯聽主至大之名。二人墮落；名逃逸；二人倒懸於天地之間直至復活日，於巴比倫教人魔術——並警誡學者：『我們是考驗，你們不要悖信。』

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend built on Qur'an 2:102; presented as the tradition's own account; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: In the Qur'an it is said: Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching men sorcery; and in Babylon the two angels Harut and Marut; and they did not teach anyone until they had said, 'We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.' The legend tells how the angels, seeing the wickedness of men, said in praise of their own obedience; and God said, 'Choose two of yourselves, and I will send you down and give you the desires of men.' Harut and Marut were chosen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Qur'an 2:102 and al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: They descended in the shape of handsome men to the gates of Babylon, and a woman named Zuhra came to them and was smitten with love; and when they turned from her she called for wine, and for idolatry, and lastly for the killing of a traveller, before she would listen to the greatest Name of God which they knew. They fell; and the Name flew up to heaven. In some tellings they hang head downward between heaven and earth, suffering until the Day of Resurrection; in Babylon they sit at a well and teach magic to all who come — but they say first, 'We are a trial; do not disbelieve.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i / al-Tha'alabi, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: The Peacock and Iblis at the Gate of the Garden
title.zh: 孔雀與易卜劣廝於樂園門前

region.en: Gate of the Garden of Eden (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊甸園門前（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Qisas al-Anbiya tradition (Arabic, c. 8th-11th centuries CE); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Muhammad al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic c. 1100); passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: Cast down, Iblis sits outside the Garden for a thousand years, unable to enter. A peacock of paradise asks him what he wants. 'I want to get in.' 'But the gate has been shut against you.' 'Tell me one thing: will the peacock's house endure for ever?' — 'No; everything but God will perish.' Iblis takes his chance: 'Show me a way in — under your foot, in your beak, in your body — and I will teach you the grain that makes death not return.' The peacock repeats it to the serpent; the serpent carries Iblis in; and paradise is opened to sorrow.
summary.zh: 易卜劣廝被逐後，於樂園外坐一千年，不得入。樂園孔雀問其所求。『我要進去。』『門已向你關閉。』『告我一事：孔雀之居將永存嗎？』——『不會；除主外萬物皆滅。』易卜劣廝乘機：『示我一入之法——足下、喙中、身內——我教你一粒穀，使死不復返。』孔雀轉告蛇；蛇攜其入；樂園自此有憂。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend of a living tradition; the peacock-serpent-Iblis dialogue is a classic of al-Kisa'i; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: When Iblis was cast out of the Garden he sat weeping at its gate for a thousand years. A peacock, one of the birds of Paradise, came and asked him why he wept. He said, 'I have been shut out of my house.' The peacock said, 'But why should you weep? The gate is shut against you.' Iblis said: 'Answer me one question: will your dwelling in the Garden endure for ever, and will you never die?' The peacock said, 'No; everything will perish except the face of God.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Iblis said, 'Show me a way into the Garden — under your foot, or in your beak, or within your body — and I will teach you a word by which you will never die, nor your children after you.' The peacock went to the serpent, who was the most beautiful of the animals, and told him; and the serpent said, 'I will carry him in within me.' So Iblis entered the Garden on the serpent's back, and whispered to Adam by the tree of eternity; and that is how death came into the world, if the legend is believed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tower of Babel in the Muslim Telling
title.zh: 穆斯林講述中的巴別塔

region.zh: 幼發拉底河畔的巴別（實際定位）

texts.period: Qisas al-Anbiya tradition (Arabic, c. 8th-11th centuries CE); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Qisas al-Anbiya / tafsir legends (al-Tabari, Tarikh; al-Tha'alabi); passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: After the Flood the children of Noah multiply in one tongue and one speech, and in the land of Babel they say: 'Let us build a tower to the sky, and fight the God of heaven.' Nimrod (in the Muslim legend, Nemrud) leads the work; fire is taken up to the top and set as a sun. God confounds their one language into seventy-two tongues; the builders can no longer understand one another, and the tower is left standing half-built as a wonder of the ancients.
summary.zh: 洪水之後，努哈子孫同語同音，於巴別之地言：『我們建塔通天，與天主作戰。』尼姆魯德（傳說中的奈姆魯德）領工；火被運至頂端，立如日。主將一語化為七十二種方言；工匠彼此不復能解，塔半成而廢，為古人奇觀。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend; the Nimrod tower narrative is an Islamic reworking of Genesis 11; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: The children of Noah multiplied after the Flood and spoke one language; and in the land of Babel they said one to another: 'Let us build a tower whose top will reach to heaven, that we may climb to it and wage war upon the God of the heaven.' And Nimrod said, 'Build'; and they built year upon year, carrying fire to the summit and setting it there as a sun, that their work might be seen from afar.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: God confounded their tongue so that one understood not the speech of another: seventy-two languages, it is said, came out of the one. The builders fell to quarrelling, and the work stopped where it stood; and the tower was left half-built as a wonder of the ancients. Some say the place of the confusion was made a city, and the city was called Babel — Bab-Il, the gate of God — because there the tongues of men were divided.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: Wadd and Suwa: Idols Made From the Memory of the Righteous
title.zh: 瓦德與素瓦：由義人記憶所造的偶像

region.en: Arabia between the Flood and Ibrahim (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 洪水與易卜拉欣之間的阿拉伯（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Qur'an 71:23 with Qisas/tafsir expansions (Arabic); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Qur'an 71:23; Qisas al-Anbiya / tafsir legends (al-Tabari); passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: Noah's people worship Wadd, Suwa, Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr; the legend says these were the names of righteous men of the generations between Adam and the Flood. When they died, Satan came to their kinsmen in the likeness of a weeping comforter and said: 'Set up a statue in the place where he used to sit, and remember him.' The images were at first honored in memory; then the next generation said: 'Our fathers worshipped them; we will worship them too.' And idols began on earth.
summary.zh: 努哈之民拜瓦德、素瓦、葉巫斯、葉歐克與奈斯爾；傳說此乃阿丹至洪水之間義人之名。其人死後，魔以哭慰者之形臨其親族：『在其常坐之處立像以為記念。』起初因記念而尊崇；下一代則言：『祖輩曾拜之，我輩亦將拜之。』偶像自此始於大地。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend built on Qur'an 71:23; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: Noah called his people night and day, and they put their fingers in their ears; and their chiefs said, 'Do not forsake your gods, and do not forsake Wadd, nor Suwa, nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr.' The legend tells that these were the names of righteous men who had lived between Adam and the Flood, whose death their people mourned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Qur'an 71:23 and al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: When one of them died, Satan came in the form of a weeping comforter and said: 'Set up a figure of him in the place where he used to sit, and set your children to play around it, that his memory may not leave you.' And they set up the images. The first generation honoured them in remembrance; but when that generation died, the next said, 'Our fathers worshipped these images; we will worship them'; and they worshipped, and made them gods. Thus idolatry began on the earth, if the legend is believed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: Sarah in the House of the King

region.en: Egypt, house of the king (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Qisas al-Anbiya / Isra'iliyat tradition (Arabic); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Qisas al-Anbiya / Isra'iliyat legends (al-Tabari, Tarikh; cf. G. Weil, The Bible, the Koran and the Talmud, 1846); passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: A famine drives Ibrahim into Egypt with Sarah, whose beauty he fears will be taken: 'Say thou art my sister.' The king's men seize her; Ibrahim prays. The king reaches out his hand, and it withers; he is told to release the woman, and is healed only after he swears. He gives her a slave-girl, Hagar, in recompense; and of Hagar comes Ismail.
summary.zh: 饑荒使易卜拉欣攜撒拉入埃及；他恐其美貌被奪：『你說是我的妹妹。』王的人捉她；易卜拉欣祈禱。王伸手，手即枯萎；被告知放人，誓後方得醫。王以婢女夏甲作償；夏甲生易司馬儀。

sensitivity.note: Qisas/Isra'iliyat legend; parallel to Genesis 12; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: When famine drove Ibrahim and Sarah into Egypt, he said to her: 'You are the fairest of women; say that you are my sister, for I fear the people of this land.' The men of the king saw her and praised her to him, and she was taken into the king's house. And Ibrahim stood in prayer; and when the king reached out his hand to her, his hand was withered as a plank.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: The king cried out, 'Pray for me, and I will not touch her.' He was healed; and he swore by God, and gave her a slave-girl named Hagar, saying: 'Take her, for I would not have aught of her.' And Sarah returned to Ibrahim; and of Hagar, who became the mother of Ismail, the lineage of the Arabs of the Hijaz descends — if the legend is believed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: Hagar, the Baby Ismail and the Water of Zamzam
title.zh: 夏甲、嬰兒易司馬儀與滲滲泉之水

texts.period: Qisas al-Anbiya / sira tradition (Arabic); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Qisas al-Anbiya / al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); cf. Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sira; passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: Ibrahim sets Hagar and the child Ismail by the House in a waterless valley and leaves; she runs twice between the hills of Safa and Marwa crying 'Water! Water!' — the origin of the sa'y rite. An angel strikes the ground and Zamzam bursts forth; she walls it with sand. The caravan of Jurhum passes, sees the bird that hangs over water, and asks leave to settle: 'Yes, so long as you do not claim the water.' Their children intermarry with Ismail's, and Mecca is founded.
summary.zh: 易卜拉欣置夏甲與幼兒易司馬儀於天房旁無水之谷而去；她於薩法與瑪爾瓦兩山間往返奔走七次，呼『水！水！』——此即賽艾之儀之源。天使擊地，滲滲泉湧出；她以沙圍之。主爾胡姆商隊見盤旋之鳥知有水，求許定居：『可以，惟不可佔水。』其子孫與易司馬儀通婚，麥加由是建立。

sensitivity.note: Qisas/sira legend of a living tradition; foundational for the Meccan sanctuary and the hajj rites; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: Ibrahim brought Hagar and her son Ismail and set them by the House, in a valley without sown land or water, and said: 'God has commanded me.' She asked, 'Then who will look after us?' He said, 'Your Lord.' And he went away; and she ran between the two hills, Safa and Marwa, seven times, seeking water for the child — and this, the legend says, is the rite of sa'y performed by every pilgrim since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: An angel struck the ground beside the child, and water burst up. Hagar scooped earth and dammed it, saying 'Zam, zam' — stay, stay; and the well of Zamzam was made. A caravan of Jurhum coming up the road saw a bird circling that never left the place — a sign of water — and asked Hagar leave to settle by the spring. She said, 'Yes, so long as you claim no right over the water.' They settled, and their children intermarried with Ismail's; and thus Mecca was founded, if the legend is believed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari, Tarikh (Arabic); not verbatim.

region.zh: 約旦希律宮廷（象徵性定位）

summary.en: Herod the tetrarch loves a woman forbidden to him by the Torah, his brother's wife. Yahya preaches against it; the woman's daughter dances before the king, and the king promises her whatever she asks; she asks for the head of Yahya on a charger. The head is brought; it speaks no more, but the tradition says the blood cried out, and the ground where it fell still bubbles, if the legend is believed.
summary.zh: 分封王希律戀慕律法所禁之女子——其兄弟之妻。葉海雅講道反對；女子之女於王前起舞，王許諾無論何求；她求葉海雅之首於盤中。首級被呈；頭不再言語，但相傳其血鳴於地，血落之處至今汩汩，如傳說所信。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend of a living tradition; the Yahya martyrdom is shared with Christian tradition; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: Herod the tetrarch desired a woman whom the Torah forbade him, the wife of his brother; and Yahya, the son of Zakariyya, preached against it. The woman contrived that her daughter should dance before the king on his feast day, and the king swore before his guests to give her whatever she asked; and she asked for the head of Yahya on a charger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: The head was brought in, and the king and his guests saw that it did not speak again; and the legend says that the blood cried out from the ground where it was spilled, and that the earth there bubbled up and has bubbled ever since, so that it was called the boiling ground. And God raised the soul of Yahya, and the prophets wept for him: 'There was not born among the children of Adam one more lawful in what he ate and more chaste than Yahya.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Well of the Water of Life
title.zh: 左勒蓋爾奈英與生命之水井

region.en: Land of darkness, beyond the sunrise (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 日出之外的黑暗之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Qisas al-Anbiya tradition (Arabic, al-Kisa'i); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Muhammad al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic c. 1100); passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: In the legend, Dhul-Qarnayn the two-horned comes at last to the land of darkness, where a well holds the water of life: whoever drinks shall not die. He enters with his cooks, each carrying a fish; the fish in one man's hand jumps into the water, and the man washes — and is granted age without end. Dhul-Qarnayn himself is not permitted: the voice tells him that death is written for him as for all. He builds his wall against Gog and Magog, and returns to his kingdom to wait for the appointed day — the Islamic cousin of Gilgamesh's plant, the quest of immortality that must fail.
summary.zh: 傳說中，雙角的左勒蓋爾奈英終至黑暗之地，其井中有生命之水：飲者不死。他攜廚師入內，各持一魚；一人手中之魚躍入水中，其人洗手——遂得不死之壽。左勒蓋爾奈英本人未蒙准許：有聲告知其死期已定，如眾人一樣。他築牆防雅朱者與馬朱者，返國等候注定之日——此即吉爾伽美什仙草的伊斯蘭親緣，注定失敗的求不死之旅。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend; the water-of-life episode parallels the Gilgamesh quest-immortality cluster; paraphrased from the Arabic original; motif tagging cross-traditional and interpretive.

passages.text: Dhul-Qarnayn travelled until he came to the land of darkness, where it is said there is a well of the water of life: whoever drinks of it does not die. He entered it with his servants, each carrying a fish; and the fish in one man's hand leapt from it into the water, and the man washed his hand — and he was granted life that does not end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: Dhul-Qarnayn himself was not permitted to drink: a voice said to him that death is written upon every son of Adam, and that his term was with his Lord. So he went out of the darkness and turned to the work God gave him — the wall of iron and copper between the peoples and Gog and Magog — and returned to his kingdom to await the appointed day. The legend makes him the seeker of the water of life who must fail, as the poets of Mesopotamia made Gilgamesh before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

title.en: The Staff of Musa: Cut From the Tree of Life
title.zh: 穆薩之杖：取自生命之樹

region.en: Garden of Eden and Tuwa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊甸園與圖窪（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Qisas al-Anbiya tradition (Arabic, al-Kisa'i); paraphrase from Arabic

source.archive: Wikisource (Arabic; al-Kisa’i, Qisas al-Anbiya, Leiden ed. 1922)
source.work: Muhammad al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic c. 1100); passages paraphrased from Arabic

texts.license: Arabic original public domain; paraphrase original

summary.en: The staff in Moses' hand, the legend says, is one of the trees of the Garden of Eden, brought down by Adam; the wood passed from prophet to prophet until God gave it to Musa, and with it the sign: cast it down and it becomes a serpent; strike the rock and twelve springs flow; part the sea with it. The staff passes out of the world when its work is done — the relic that binds Eden, Sinai and the Exodus in a single object.
summary.zh: 相傳穆薩手中之杖乃伊甸園諸樹之一，由阿丹帶下；此木自先知傳至先知，直至主賜穆薩；並賜其兆：擲之則化蛇；擊石則湧十二泉；持之分海。其功既成，杖遂離世——此一聖物將伊甸、西奈與出埃及繫於一物。

sensitivity.note: Qisas legend of a living tradition; the staff's Edenic origin is popular lore; paraphrased from the Arabic original.

passages.text: The staff that Musa carried, the legend says, was cut from one of the trees of the Garden of Eden, and brought down by Adam when he was expelled; and the wood was handed down from prophet to prophet, from Adam to Idris to Nuh, until God gave it to Musa in the valley of Tuwa.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.

passages.text: With it God gave him his signs: cast it down before Pharaoh and it becomes a serpent that swallows the serpents of the magicians; strike the rock with it and twelve springs gush out, one for each tribe; stretch it over the sea and the waters stand like walls. And when the work of Musa was finished the staff went out of the world, and is not found — for it was, the legend says, the last relic of the Garden among men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Kisa'i, Qisas al-Anbiya (Arabic); not verbatim.
